text: We're going to describe a class of tests called permutation tests, and in particular two-sample permutation tests. Now permutation tests are a family of tests which are at least when sample sizes are not small, they're computationally intensive. Luckily today we have software available and the software package R provides commands for performing permutation tests. Well, we'll illustrate with an example. An example is a US trial, a civil trial, a discrimination case from 1981, and the plaintiff was named Andrea Capacci, and she brought a case to the court against her employers, Katz and Besthoff, Inc. Now you can Google this trial if you like. And this trial was a sexual discrimination trial, and as part of the evidence there were data presented about times to promotion in months for men and women in the company over a period of time. So, for the men's times to promotion, the figures in order were something like this, 5, 7, 12, 40, 40, won't give the full data here. There were 22 promotion times for men, and the sample size was 483. So let's say N1 sample size for the men was 22. There were only actually two women who got promoted, and their promotion times were 229 and 453. So, what would our null hypothesis be here? Well, we'll return to the notion of the extent of inference in general, just at the end of this little lecture. We noticed that really the data here are not samples, they represent the complete data that were available for individuals who were promoted over a particular time period. The time period itself is a form of a sample, but given the time period was determined by the duration of time that the plaintiff Kapachi had been in the employment of the company, that was kind of fixed. So, the process by which the data give rise to the the the process by which these promotion times are created, I suppose, is the the essence of what we're interested in. And whatever the processes were, they give rise to some data, we've observed the data. The null hypothesis would be that the distribution of times to promotion for men and women were the same over the time period in question. This would, of course, imply that they have the same means, the same medians. What would we take as the alternative hypothesis? Well, for sure, the distributions are different, which would simply be the negation of the null hypothesis. But I would argue here that one should consider only a one-sided alternative. The one-sided alternative being that the women's promotion times are greater, on average. So, the distribution of the distribution of the women's promotion times was, on average, larger. So, I had a greater mean, say, or greater median than that for the men. Now, why would I take a one-sided case here? I would argue that, given that this is a discrimination trial, it is inconceivable that a case would make it to the court for a claim for discrimination against women, gender discrimination, where in fact there was evidence that there was positive discrimination, or it was plausible, in any way, that there was positive discrimination towards women. Hence, I consider here the only logical alternative one can take to the null is an alternative which is one-sided. And that is the case that we will consider. So, what do we do in a permutation test? Well, we choose some test statistic or other. So, what should I choose as a test statistic? You can pretty much choose anything that would be a sensible choice. I'm going to choose something very simple. The sum of the women's promotion times, which in this case is 229 plus 453 is 682. That might strike you as being an odd choice for test statistic, just the sum of the data for the women. In fact, I'd get exactly the same inference inference here, if I chose the sample means, the difference in the sample means of the test statistic, or even the t statistic. So, if you were doing a two-sample t-test here, well, you've only got two observations for the women's group, but you could do a two-sample t-test, and I'd get the same inference, actually. I think I'm at it saying. So, the question we ask ourselves is, we have data, we have data for men, and we have data for women, and we have 22 observations for the men, and two for the women's, so 24 observations in total, two of which were women's, and 22 were men. So, we ask ourselves, well, how many, I'll say regroupings, are there, of 24 observations, where we put two in one group, and 22 in another? Well, the answer is, of course, 24 choose 2. So, 24 observations. I don't really care about the ordering in each group, I just care about how many ways I can put two in one group and 22 in another. And if we work that out, that comes to 276. So, there are 276 ways of taking 24 numbers and putting two in one group, call that the women, and 22 in the other. And under the null hypothesis, well, all of those regroupings should be equally likely. Now, the question that we ask is, how many of those give a value of the test statistic at least as inconsistent as the one that we've observed, which is 682? Well, we can enumerate them. In particular, the one that we observed, so we always include that one. So, that was the one that we observed. What else might we have observed? Well, we might have observed 229 and 483. We might have observed 453 and 483, the two largest values. So, those three ways to group our data to give a test statistic at least as inconsistent with the null hypothesis as the one that we observed. So, how do we find our p-value? Well, our p-value says, well, actually there were 276 ways, all of which should be equally likely of grouping the data, of which three gave a value at least as inconsistent as the one we observed. Of course, that includes the one we observed. And given that we're doing a one-tailed test, the p-value is just based on that tail, and we have a p-value of 0.01, so around 1%. So, that's quite strong evidence against the null hypothesis that the men and women's promotion times were from the same distribution. Notice that if we did a two-tailed test, we'd also arrive at a conclusion that there was evidence, although a little less strong, against the null hypothesis. Let's talk in generality now, and describe what we've done in the general case, where we've got two samples of size, let's call them M and N, respectively. So, I choose a test statistic. You can simply choose a test statistic that is a test statistic for a test that you already know, so you could choose a two-sample-t-test statistic, or rank sum, or whatever. We find, at least in principle, the test statistic that we chose for all of the n plus m to n regroupings of the data. So, all the ways in which we can assign the n plus m numbers into a group of n and a group of m. find the number of samples that have a test statistic at least as inconsistent with the null hypothesis as not observed. It's the one that we saw. And we divide that number so that count by n plus m to n to give our p-value. So, let's just talk a little bit more about our example in this Apache case. So, the data in the trial was such that if we choose t as our test statistic, let's say it's the total of the women's promotion times. We notice that if we look back at our data, the smallest value that could have taken across the regroupings is when the two smallest observations were for the women, which were five and seven. So, there's one out of the 276 groupings that gives a value of 12 for our test statistic. The next smallest value is 17. Again, there's only one way to do that. The next smallest value is 19 and actually there's quite a few ways that can arise and so on. So, we get different numbers of ways. So, remember, this is the sampling distribution of this test statistic under the null hypothesis and we actually observed something way up in the upper tail, 682, and we were doing a one tail test and those three cases together would only have probability of about 0.1 if all of these possibilities, all of the 276 were equally likely. So, that seems large, it seems to be way up in the upper tail if, in fact, T really was following this distribution under our null hypothesis. So, as always, when we're performing a test, we're considering how does that test statistic behave if the null hypothesis was true? And here, we're doing a brute force approach. We're actually computing this sampling distribution explicitly. We're really only interested in the tails, but we should have this picture in our mind. Interestingly enough, the Capacci case was defeated even, I understand, after an appeal. Of course, although these data look compelling, there's more to the data than meets the eye. There's always a story behind our data. And, of course, the data only included information for people who made it to promotion. So, there's no information about people who served the company and who didn't get promoted in that time. And there was also evidence that there were women who had turned down promotion, so had been offered promotion but refused it. I think on the grounds that the nature of the work changed once they got promoted and didn't suit some women. So, although the data looked quite, these data looked quite convincing, the case was defeated in the event. Now, let's just conclude here with a brief talk about the extent of statistical inference. Because, as we described in this example, the data were not a sample. So, normally, when we're doing statistics, we're thinking to ourselves that we have some sort of population, so some sort of set of individuals or objects or something, and we take a sample from that population. We hope, or it should be hoped, that we take the sample in some sensible way as to minimise bias. And a simple random sample, rather like a lottery or raffle, is the optimal type of sample to take. And if we were to take such a sample, then we'd be probably quite happy in drawing inference about our sample back to the population. More often, particularly when we're dealing with populations of human beings, it's very difficult to take a true random sample like a lottery. Now, in the Capaccio case, the data were not a sample. So, the inference, if anything, was about the process which gave rise to the promotion times. So, whatever the processes were, or if there was a single process, really did it differ for the men and the women. So, we can imagine some mechanism, some pseudo-random process which is giving rise to the data, and we were interested in, well, however this process operated, is it giving the same sort of data for men as it did for women? So, there was no sample there as such, unless one thinks of hypothetical individuals who might have worked for the company but didn't, and their promotion times we weren't observed, but we actually observed some subset of people who did work for the company. Now, extending the idea a little further, we'll discuss in the course examples of what we would describe as experiments. So, sometimes we don't just stop at taking a sample and observing what we've seen from the sample, we do some sort of experiment, and an experiment involves, in the simplest form, just applying some treatments to our sample. Now, sample individuals tend to be called experimental units, or, less dispassionately if they're human beings, subjects, and we would hope, in a nice experiment, to allocate experimental units to treatments at random. And a well-designed experiment will be such that, well, however we've got our experimental units, which will almost always be by some sort of sampling procedure, then we have randomisation in that we randomly allocate individuals to treatments. So, for example, if we had a sample of cancer patients, so a sample of individuals who all suffer from, let's say, colon cancer, and we have some different treatments to test, then we would randomise patients to treatments. So, this would be done, hopefully, in a double blind way, the patients don't know what treatment they're getting, and the doctors making the diagnosis don't know what sort of treatment they're getting either. A little more on that later. Now, in that case, it probably doesn't matter a great deal how the sample were obtained, so long as there's randomisation in the allocation of patients to treatment, we can make inference from our data, so we measure some responses, we can make inference about the treatments. Whether we can then extend that to the population, well, that may be a little more tenuous because it may not be that the sample of individuals in our experiment were a random sample of all possible, well, individuals in the so-called target population. but even if the sample were biased in some way, we would hope that randomisation will still give appropriate inference about the treatments, whether we could extend to the whole target population, I mean, there may be, for example, subsets of the target population which were for some reason excluded from the possibility of appearing in our set of experimental subjects, experimental units, then we may not be able to make the inference that this will always apply to all members of the population, but the treatments we may be able to draw conclusions about. In the ideal world, we would have a random sample from our population and in an experiment randomly assign individuals to treatments, and then we really, we'd be quite happy to do a, in the ideal case, we'd be quite happy to do a permutation test in those cases, we probably don't need any statistical model to describe the variable that we're measuring, and in that case, a permutation test is simply dubbed a randomisation test just to make it clear that there was randomisation in the allocation of the units to the treatment. It's just a permutation test. the mechanism by which the test is performed is really just the same. So, permutation tests, sometimes known also as randomisation tests, are very powerful tests, powerful in the sense of they can be applied in a wide range of scenarios, they give an exact inference, but they are computationally intensive. We have computers these days, and the history of statistics would have looked rather different had the grandfathers and grandmothers of the subject had the computational power that we have available to us today. So that's a little bit about permutation tests. I hope you understood it and enjoyed it.
